references.text: The Mosaic law requires that an executed person hung on a tree be taken down before evening, so as not to defile the land. Joshua followed this law by taking down the five kings before evening.
Joshua did the same with the king of Ai—hanging him on a tree until evening and taking him down at sunset. This shows a repeated pattern in Joshua's treatment of defeated kings.
The broader context of the event, where the five kings hid in the cave at Makkedah, were captured, and then executed and hung on trees.
David had the hands and feet of Rekab and Baana cut off and hung them by the pool in Hebron, another example of public hanging of enemies as a form of justice.
Paul quotes Deuteronomy 21:23 and explains that Christ became a curse for us by being hung on a tree, connecting the Old Testament practice of hanging with Christ's atoning death.
Peter refers to Christ bearing our sins on the tree, using the image of being hung on a tree to describe the crucifixion and its saving significance.
